book.title: A Dictionary of English and Welsh Surnames, with Special American Instances
book.author: Charles Wareing Bardsley

headwords.meaning: the son of Aaron
headwords.author_comment: A Jewish surname settled in England. I have not met with a single English Aaron in mediaeval times.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam (Welsh ap- or ab-Adam)
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bethell, Bloyd, Breeze, &c.

headwords.meaning: (1) at the Abbey, from residence thereby; (2) from the ecclesiastical title
headwords.author_comment: All the evidence is in favour of this view except in one instance.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham, or Abell, from the nick. Abb, with double dim. Abb-in-et
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Robinet and Colinet.

headwords.meaning: variant of Abbs
headwords.author_comment: V. Abbs, of which, no doubt, it is a variant.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Abraham, from the nick. Abb, and dim. Abb-ot; (2) the Abbot, an official title or nickname
headwords.author_comment: It is all but certain that the majority of our Abbotts, although bearing a conventual title, are thus descended [from Abraham]. Abraham was a favourite name in the 13th century. Abel was also popular, and may have shared the parentage.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham or Abel, from nick. Abb or Abbie
headwords.author_comment: This was a familiar Norfolk surname as Abbys or Abbes. To-day it is familiar in the same county as Abbs.

headwords.meaning: of the Abdy; query, an old form of 'Abbey' (?)
headwords.author_comment: Lower says: 'Abdy, an estate in Yorkshire, where the family anciently resided.' This is corroborated by the following entries. All these [1379 entries] were living at Brampton-juxta-Wath. The 'del' is interesting.

headwords.meaning: at the Beck-head, from residence at the head or source of the beck
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birkett, originally Birk-head, or Birkenhead, the head of the birch-trees. Birkett is a Cumberland surname. Birkenhead, co. Chester, is but a variant, being the adjectival form; v. Beck. Cf. Roger a'Hulle (co. Oxf., 1273. A.), i.e. Roger at the Hill.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel
headwords.author_comment: Much more popular in mediaeval society than in that of the 19th century. Among the peasantry, however, Abel still receives a certain amount of attention as a font-name.
headwords.modern_distribution: Boston (U.S.), 58, 10, 2, 0, 0; London, 7, 8, 1, 1, 0; MDB. (N. Rid. Yorkshire), Able 1

headwords.meaning: Ab-Ithel (Welsh), i.e. the son of Ithel
headwords.author_comment: v. Bethell, and cf. Abadam.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel, from dim. Abel-ot
headwords.author_comment: A feminine form occurs in the Hundred Rolls; v. infra.

headwords.meaning: doubtless a corruption of Applethwaite, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Hebblewhite.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel, from the dim. Abel-in
headwords.author_comment: v. Aplin (2).

headwords.headword: Abraham, Abrahams, Abrahamson, Abram, Abrams, Abramson
headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Abraham; (2) of Abram, a township in the parish of Wigan, Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: (1) A popular font-name in the 13th century; v. Abbot. In the Fen district especially the entries are common. The instances in the Hundred Rolls are all but entirely confined to the Fen counties. A glance at the London Directory will show that in general Abraham represents the old English stock, and Abrahams the more modern Jewish. This is proved by comparing the personal or Christian names prefixed to the instances; cf. Solomon and Salmon. (2) Abram was originally written Adburgham. The Lancashire Abram and Abraham spring from this place.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abrahee, presumably a form of Abraham
the son of Absolom
headwords.author_comment: A fairly popular font-name in the 13th century, and not confined to the Jews. 'Now was ther of that chirche a parish clerk, The which that was ycleped Absolon.' Chaucer, C. T. 3312.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham; v. Abbs
at the burn, corrupted to Aburn
headwords.author_comment: Cf. A'Becket, A'Wood, &c.

headwords.meaning: see Cator (a buyer of victuals)
headwords.author_comment: Chaucer says of the manciple who was so 'wise in buying of victuals,' that of him 'Achatours mighten take ensample.'

headwords.meaning: the son of Achard
headwords.author_comment: v. Hatchard.

headwords.meaning: see Atkirk
the Acreman: a ploughman, a husbandman, a tiller of the soil
headwords.author_comment: 'both prestis and knightis mosten bicome acremen and heerdis,' 1389: Hist. Eng. Dic. 'The foules up, and song on bough, And acremen yede to the plough.' Lay le Freine, 176 (Halliwell). Akermann is of German birth.

headwords.meaning: at the Ackley, i.e. the oak-meadow
headwords.author_comment: The exact equivalent of Oakley, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Acklam, two parishes in co. York, one in the union of Malton, the other in the union of Stockton
of the Ackroyd, i.e. the oak clearing
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Ormerod, Murgatroyd, &c. A well-known Yorkshire surname.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 28, 2, 0, 2, 6; MDB. (W. Riding), 17, 0, 1, 4, 0; Philadelphia, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: of Acland (Ac or Oakland, named from a large grove of oaks; Saxon ac)
headwords.author_comment: 'From the situation of their ancient seat in Lankey, near Barnstaple, co. Devon, which, being in the midst of a large grove of oaks (in Saxon ac), obtained the name of Ac or Oakland. ... They were settled in this place as early as the reign of Henry II.' (Lower, quoting Kimber's Baronetage.)
headwords.modern_distribution: Exeter, 1, 2; MDB. (co. Devon), 3, 2; London, 4, 6; Philadelphia, 0, 2; Boston, 0, 3

headwords.meaning: the son of Alcock (q.v.), corrupted to Accock, which took the imitative form of Haycock
headwords.author_comment: At least it would appear so. If we could find any instances of Halcock representing Henry, we should then be obliged to refer the three last to that personal name.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Acomb, a parish near York; (2) of Acomb, two townships in the union of Hexham, co. Northumberland
variant of Acock
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Glasscock for Glasscott.

headwords.meaning: of the Acre, or Acres, from residence beside the field or fields called the Acre or Acres
of Acton, i.e. the farmstead among the oaks
headwords.author_comment: There are in England no less than sixteen parishes, hamlets, townships, &c., called Acton.

headwords.meaning: of Ackworth, a parish near Wakefield, co. York
the son of Adam
headwords.author_comment: Almost the prime favourite as a font-name in the 13th century; v. Addis, Adcock, Atkins, Atkinson, Addyman, &c. Adams is remarkably well represented in the United States. A single glance at the Index to Hotten's Lists of Emigrants will suffice to show that many Adams, Addams, Adamsons, or Addamsons were among the early settlers.

headwords.meaning: of Adamthwaite (i.e. the clearing of Adam the first settler, probably in the 12th century), a small hamlet in Ravenstonedale, co. Westm.
headwords.author_comment: v. Thwaites.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ade with suffix -cock
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Wilcock, Jeffcock, Watcock, &c.; v. Addis with Atcock; cf. Atkins for Adkins.

headwords.meaning: of Atherley, a parish in co. Salop, pronounced Adderley
the son of Adam, from an early dim. (?)
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Adnett and Adnitt, q.v.

headwords.headword: Addis, Addison, Adds, Addy, Ade, Ades, Adey, Adie, Ady, Addey, Aday, Adee
headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ad, Ade, or Addy
headwords.author_comment: All are reminders of the wonderful popularity of Adam in the north of England, if not in the south; cf. Adcock and Adkin, q.v. A common entry in the Hundred Rolls [of the 'fil. Ade' form]. With the variant Adice cf. Ellice for Ellis, or Bevance for Bevans.

headwords.meaning: the servant or knave of Addy, i.e. Adam
headwords.author_comment: v. Addy and Addison. This is decidedly interesting. It is one of the chief witnesses to-day of the existence of the class of surnames to which it belongs. As a matter of course its home is in Yorkshire; cf. Mathewman, Peterman, Perryman, Jackman, Bartleman, &c. In the following entries, although Ade (i.e. Addy) is given as the nick. of Adam, the entry is unfortunately in Latin. In English it would have read Thomas and Johannes Addyman. We are more fortunate in a further instance, where the English form is given.

headwords.meaning: see Addis

headwords.headword: Adkin, Adkins, Adkinson, Atkin, Atkins, Atkinson, Atkyns, Adkisson
headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Addy, dim. Adkin, sharpened to Atkin
headwords.author_comment: There is no need of course to prove this, but it is interesting to note the following: 'Adam le Fullere,' a citizen of London, is twice referred to as Adekin le Fullere (1273, Hundred Rolls, i. 426). Six centuries ago Adam probably ranked as second or third favourite among boys' names throughout England. In the north it attained a most remarkable pre-eminence. Four Adams are mentioned in the revenues of Conishead Priory, A.D. 1256 (West's Furness, pp. 192, 195). No fewer than six Adams figure as benefactors of Furness Abbey, circa 1290 (ibid.). The everyday form was Adekin, then Adkin, and finally Atkin (see Addison). The following come together [Johannes Attekyson and Alicia soror Adekynson].

headwords.meaning: see Adnam
the son of Adelard or Athelard
headwords.author_comment: v. Allard. Adelhard was a cousin of Charlemagne, and Abbot of Corbie. (Yonge, ii. 399.)

headwords.meaning: the son of Adeline, alias Atheline
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Athelard and Adlard.

headwords.meaning: of Addingham; parishes in co. Cumberland and W. Rid. Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Swetnam and Swetman for Swettenham, or Debnam and Deadman for Debenham, or Putnam and Putman for Puttenham. Adlam is a further and natural variant; cf. bannister for baluster. With Adnum, cf. Barnum for Barnham.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Addy, dim. Add-in, second dim. Add-in-et
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Addinson, q.v. Adin or Addin was evidently the O.F. equivalent of Adkin, the customary English form; v. Atkins and Atkinson.

headwords.meaning: local origin (?) - uncertain
the son of Adrian
headwords.author_comment: The form Adrain is an old one. The sheriff, John Adrian, entered below, is recorded as John Adrain: A. i. p. 403.

headwords.meaning: of Adshead, some spot in the neighbourhood of Prestbury, co. Chester
headwords.author_comment: Prestbury church register teems with entries relating to the family. The surname has crossed the Atlantic.

headwords.meaning: of Auchinleck, N.B. (North Britain, i.e. Scotland)
headwords.author_comment: 'A singular contraction of the surname Auchinleck, borne by an ancient family "of that ilk" in Ayrshire. Sir Edmund Affleck, created baronet in 1782, was sixth in descent from Sir John Auchinleck, son of Gilbert A. of Auchinleck': Lower, Pat. Brit., p. 3.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agar, or Ager
headwords.author_comment: Probably a form of Algar, a Domesday personal name, and very popular for several centuries; v. Algar.

headwords.meaning: see Haggard
headwords.author_comment: Arthur Agard, a distinguished antiquary, was descended of an old Derbyshire family. He was born in 1540, and died in 1615. He was one of the original members of the Society of Antiquaries, and was buried in Westminster Abbey. (Dict. Nat. Biog. i. 173, and Stanley's Westminster Abbey, p. 443.) Haggard is the usual form of this patronymic.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agace; a form of Agatha
(1) at the gate, from residence thereby; (2) the son of Agnes, from the nick. Agg, dim. Agot
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Atwood, Bywater, &c.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agnes, from the nick. Agg
headwords.author_comment: Aggie is still the favourite north English nick.

headwords.meaning: a corruption of Acland, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Ackland, Acland, and Agland are all found indifferently in co. Devon, the home of the name; v. Devon Directory; cf. the Lancashire Ogden for Oakden.

headwords.meaning: of Aglionby, a township in the parish of Warwick, three miles from Carlisle, co. Cumb.
a needler, a maker of needles (O.F. aguille, a needle)
headwords.author_comment: 'A silver needle forth I drew / Out of an aguiler quaint ynow.' Chaucer, Rom. Rose, 98. O.F. aguille, a needle.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ade and dim. Adkin
headwords.author_comment: The Scotch form of Atkin, q.v., was Aitkin. This was further corrupted to Aiken and Aikin.

headwords.meaning: see Askew
of Annesley, a parish in co. Notts, near Nottingham
headwords.author_comment: But there is probably a north English local origin also. There is also Ansley, a parish in co. Warwick.

headwords.meaning: of Ainsworth, a chapelry in the parish of Middleton, co. Lanc., formerly Aynesworth
of Airey
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot, but the family arose in co. Cumberland or Westmoreland. Almost every instance can be traced back to one or other county.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Auskettle, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Probably a modified form. On the other hand it may be local, with the suffix -gill, so common to the narrow gorges of the northern counties.

headwords.meaning: of Aislaby, (1) a township in the parish of Egglescliffe, co. Durh.; (2) a chapelry in the parish of Whitby, N.R. Yorks, formerly Aslakeby (v. Aslac); hence 'the dwelling of Aslac,' the first settler
headwords.author_comment: 'Aislabie, one of the oldest names in the county of Durham, from Aislaby, a parish on the river Tees, on the banks of which the family still reside. In old documents it is written Ashlackby, and in about fifty other modes' (Lower).

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Archibald (?), from the nick. Archie, a Scotch Border favourite; t intrusive, as in Ritchie, from same district; (2) the son of Adkin, q.v.: a Border form of the great north English surname Atkinson
headwords.author_comment: (1) t intrusive, as in Ritchie, from same district, q.v. (2) A Border form of the great north English surname Atkinson. This is the true source of the majority of our Aitchesons, &c. Atshison = Atkinson: Dickinson's Glossary of the Words and Phrases of Cumberland, p. 4.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam; the Scotch Border form of Atkin, q.v.
a variant of Hazlewood, q.v.
at the oak-head (from residence thereby), the top or furthest reach of the oak-trees
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birk-head, now Birkett; and v. Akenhead for further instances.

headwords.meaning: v. Akenside
headwords.author_comment: Lower says, 'Akenhead: Akenside - doubtless local; from Aiken, an early proprietor.' This latter statement is wholly incorrect.

headwords.meaning: of Akenside, i.e. the side of the clump of oak-trees; A.S. acen; cf. Beechen, Linden, Birchen, with the adjectival suffix -en
headwords.author_comment: The place, whether a manor or mere farmstead, is distinctly set down in the list of landed proprietors in Hodgson's Hist. of Northumberland (iv. 268). Akenside, the poet, it will be remembered, was born at Newcastle-on-Tyne in 1721. His parentage and descent, therefore, were strictly local, and his 'forbears' had wandered but a few miles from their original home; cf. Thomas Carlyle and the city Carlisle (v. Carlisle). -side is a common suffix of north English local names, used in the same sense as lake-side, pit-side; cf. Fawcett or Garside, q.v. Also, cf. Adam de Birkinside, 1322: E. and F., co. Cumb. p. 165. Akenhead, i.e. at the head of the oak-trees, corresponds with Birkenhead, Birkett, and Beckett, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Acaster, two parishes of this name near York
headwords.author_comment: This surname has crossed from Yorkshire into Furness, Lancashire.

headwords.meaning: the Arbalester, i.e. cross-bowman; O.F. arbalestier; v. H.E.D.
headwords.author_comment: Illustrated by verses from Robert of Gloucester ('Spearmen anote, and bowemen, and also arblasters') and Chaucer, Rom. Rose, 4196 ('Of arblasters great plentie were').

headwords.meaning: (1) de Albini, not the Scotch Albany; (2) the son of Alban, popularly Albany
headwords.author_comment: (1) 'William de Albini attended William the Conqueror. Wace mentions him as "the butler d'Aubignie"' (Lower). Hence the Earls of Arundel. (2) This form has survived in some districts till to-day.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albert, from Ethelbert or Adelbert; German Albrecht
headwords.author_comment: v. also Allbright for further instances. The Albrechts of the London Dir. are all of late German immigration. Also the Albrechts of Philadelphia.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Albray, probably Aubrey; (2) of Aldbury, a parish in co. Hertfordshire, three miles from Tring
headwords.author_comment: v. Albury for other instances.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albin or Alban; pet form Albany, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Earlier still, in 1269, we find one Albin de Dereby forbidden to dwell within the precincts of London city: WWW. p. 125. For other examples see next article.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albin, or Alban; v. Albin
headwords.author_comment: The following entry [1790, Jane Alberson] has probably no connexion with Alberston. With this variant cf. Patterson for Pattinson.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban; v. Allbon
of Albury, or Aldborough, parishes in cos. Norfolk, Suffolk, York (W.R.), York (E.R.), and Hertford
headwords.author_comment: v. Eldborough.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albot, probably a popular form of Albrecht; v. Albert
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 0, 2; Philadelphia, 0, 1

headwords.meaning: the son of Allen, from the pet form Allicock or Allcock; v. Cock, and cf. Wilcock, Jeffcock, Simcock
headwords.author_comment: 'The same holds one messuage which formerly belonged to Matilda Alcoke, doghtyr.' 'The same holds one tenement which formerly belonged to Alcoke of Hynganderode': Rental of Halifax (1439), Cotton MSS. Vespasian; F. 15, Brit. Mus. Mr. Lower says this name is a dim. of Hal, the nick. of Henry. The evidence is against this view; v. Allkin. There is clear proof that the original form was Alycock, and that this was abbreviated to Al-cock. Allen would readily take the nick. Ally or Aly, and the suffix -cock was added as a matter of course. The important point is to remember the enormous popularity of Allen in the 13th and 14th centuries, and the absolute certainty that both nick. and pet forms would be in everyday use.

headwords.meaning: of Aldham, q.v.
the son of Aldwin; i.e. Aylwin, with intrusive d
headwords.author_comment: 'This town (Shelton, co. Norf.) in the Confessor's time belonged to Bishop Stigand, and was held of him by Aldwin, or Alwin': FF. v. 263. The surname was common in the 13th century, but, like every other of the numerous compounds of -win, settled into -en, -in, and -ing; cf. Golden, Goldin, Goulding. Audenshaw, a division of Ashton-under-Lyne, was originally Aldwinshaigh, i.e. the wood of Aldwin.

headwords.meaning: at the alder-tree; from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Ash, Nash, Birch, Rowntree, &c. The plural is found in the two entries following [Thomas and Henry in the Alren]. 'Aldren = elders': Halliwell. Thus the d in Alder is excrescent.

headwords.meaning: the alderman, probably used sometimes personally
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bateman, Tiddyman, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Aldersey, a township in the parish of Coddington, near Chester
headwords.author_comment: This is settled beyond controversy by the following entries. The grandfather of Anne and Margaret Aldersey was 'John Aldersey, of Aldersey, co. Chester,' who married Anne Low, sister of Sir Thomas Low, alderman of London. Their father was Samuel Aldersey, of London, haberdasher: v. Visitation of London, 1633-4, p. 8.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldus (v. Aldhous), a once familiar personal name
headwords.author_comment: Aldus-son would soon settle down into Alderson.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 11; West Rid. Court Dir., 7; Philadelphia, 3

headwords.meaning: of Aldham, probably an early form of Oldham, co. Lanc., on the borders of Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: There are, however, parishes of this name in cos. Essex and Suffolk.

headwords.headword: Aldhouse, Aldhous, Aldis, Aldous, Aldus, Alldiss
headwords.meaning: the son of Aldus
headwords.author_comment: Not local, as several of its corrupted forms would seem to prove. These are simply imitative. The documentary proofs are extremely strong. Norfolk has been a long-established home for this name, both in its fontal and patronymic character.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldith, an early form of Edith (?)
the son of Aldred
headwords.author_comment: This personal name died out soon after the surname epoch, and instances of its occurrence as a fontal name are scarce.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alderich
headwords.author_comment: Although wearing a local guise, it is easy to see that Aldridge belongs to the baptismal class.

headwords.meaning: of Aldwinkle, a parish three miles from Thrapston, co. Northampton
of Aldworth, a parish in co. Berks, near Wantage
the alefounder, an inspector appointed by the Court Leet to assize and supervise the brewing of malt liquor
headwords.author_comment: Another term for this office was ale-conner. A poem of James I's reign says-'A nose he had that gan show, What liquor he loved I trow; For he had before long seven years Been of the towne the ale-conner.' A confirmation by John, Abbot of Cockerham, Lancashire, 1 Ric. III, says, in regulating the price of beer, 'Yai sall gyf Ale-fwnders a fwnding galon or else a taste of ylke vessell,' &c.; Baines' Lanc. ii. 588. This word is neither in Halliwell nor in the Hist. Eng. Dictionary; cf. 'fondyn, or asayyn-attempto,' Prompt. Parv. p. 169. Way adds in a note: 'A.S. fandian, tentare.' Lower quotes from the Norfolk Chronicle, Aug. 19, 1854, a Court Leet of the Borough of New Buckenham at which 'the sub-bailiff, affiers, searchers, and sealers of leather, examiners of fish and flesh, alefounders, inspectors of weights and measures, and a pinder were appointed': Patr. Brit. p. 5. Again Lower quotes from Three Early Metr. Rom. (Camden Soc.), p. xxxviii: 'In the records of the manor of Hale in the xvth cent. one Thomas Layet is mentioned as being fined ... for having concealed the founding pot (quia concelavit le fowundynge pot), 3d.' Evidently the official term as well as the surname were in existence in Norfolk till a very recent period.

headwords.meaning: the ale-tunner, one who filled tuns or casks with ale
headwords.author_comment: v. Turner and Tunneler.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alexander
headwords.author_comment: v. Saunders. This personal name is common to all Europe, and in England was an early favourite. Stories of prodigious achievements, many of them miraculous, caused it to be immensely admired. Miss Yonge (i. 199-202) quotes Chaucer as saying-'Alisaundres storie is commune, That everie wight that hath discrecion Hath herde somewhat.' 'Alysaunder, propyr name Alexander': Prompt. Parv.

headwords.meaning: of Alford; parishes in cos. Linc. and Somerset, and no doubt smaller spots in various counties, as meaning 'the old ford'
headwords.author_comment: For the form Alforth, v. Forth.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alfred, or Alured
headwords.author_comment: This latter form is still found as a surname, although Alfred has long been the accepted orthography of the fontal name. It is curious that Alfred has so few representatives in the directories. Where Allen occupies columns, Alfred occupies lines.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alfrey, i.e. Alfred
headwords.author_comment: Alfried, Alfred, Alfrey; cf. Godfrey, Godfried, Humfrey, Humfreid: Yonge, i. pp. lxviii and lxxviii.

headwords.meaning: the son of Algar, or Alfgar
headwords.author_comment: In Domesday commonly found as Algar. It is also met with alone without surname attached in the Hundred Rolls, ii. 472. This surname is a familiar one as Algar in co. Norfolk. It is early found there both as a personal and a surname. Algar, although forgotten now, was evidently popular in its day and generation; cf. the place-name Algersthorp, co. Norf.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Alice; (2) the son of Alice, from the popular dim. Alison; (3) the son of Allen, corrupted from Allenson
headwords.author_comment: (2) cf. Marion from Mary, Gibbon from Gib (i.e. Gilbert), Beaton from Beatrice, &c. 'This Alison answered: Who is there That knocketh so?' Chaucer, C. T. 3788. (3) Such a corruption was bound to take place; cf. Pattinson and Pattison. There can be no doubt many of our Allisons are traceable to this source. For early instances, v. Allenson. Allison has ramified very strongly in the United States.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 15; West Rid. Court Dir., 0, 6; Philadelphia, 0, 86

headwords.meaning: of Altcar, a village six miles from Ormskirk, co. Lancaster
headwords.author_comment: This surname is rarely found outside the county. Its origin is easily proved by the following instances.

headwords.meaning: see Allkins
see Allman; cf. Lallimand
the son of Alard, abbreviated from Adelard
headwords.author_comment: v. Adlard.

headwords.meaning: of Allardyce, an estate in the parish of Arbuthnot, co. Kincardine, N.B.
the son of Elliot, q.v., the dim. of Ellis
see Allvey, Alloway
headwords.author_comment: This is a natural variant, the intrusive a being euphonic; cf. Greenaway, Hathaway, Ottaway, &c.

headwords.meaning: variant of Alabaster
headwords.author_comment: An American variant.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban, patr. Albans
headwords.author_comment: v. Albinson. In the register of the parish church, Bolingbroke, Albans in the 17th century is represented by Allbones in the 19th; v. Allibone, Alban, and Albany. 'Stol'n from mine host of S. Albones': Falstaff, 1 Hen. IV, iv. 2.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ailbrit; in Domesday Ailbriht
headwords.author_comment: Albrecht is a German immigrant of much later date. Allbright is English. Albert, again, is ancient and modern. For other instances, v. Albert.

headwords.meaning: variant of Albutt
(1) the son of Alcuin (v. Yonge, ii. 350), corrupted to Oldcorn in north England; (2) of Alchorne, a manor in the parish of Rotherfield, co. Sussex, where the family lived in the 14th century
headwords.author_comment: I have one representative in my parish (Ulverston). I place all these surnames together because it is impossible to separate them. No doubt both (2) and (1) have assimilated. In a general way Alchorn represents the local, and Alcorn the personal surname. (2) Some of their descendants, still resident in that parish, have, within a generation or two, corrupted their name to Allcorn (Lower).

headwords.meaning: see Holdcroft
the son of Aldy, a popular form of Aldwin, or Aldred, or Aldrich, or Aldus, or some other of the once popular compounds of Ald
headwords.author_comment: But the probable ancestor was Aldwin, which was early modified into Aldwy; v. Allvey.

headwords.headword: Allen, Alleine, Alleyne, Allan, Allin, Alland
headwords.meaning: the son of Alan, or Allen, or Aleyn (Yonge, i. 396-7)
headwords.author_comment: 'Aleyne, propyr name, Alanus': Prompt. Parv. 'Forth goth Alein, the clerk, and also John.'—Chaucer, C. T. 4015. (The d in Alland is an excrescence as in Simmonds.) One of our most popular names while surnames were becoming hereditary; said to have come into England with Alan Fergéant, Count of Brittany, a companion of the Conqueror, and first Earl of Richmond, co. York. Very soon common to north England and the Scottish border. The founder of Dulwich Coll., 1619, was Edward Allen, or Alleyne. Derivatives, Allcock, Allkins, Allnutt, and perhaps Allatt, q.v. Possibly an abbrev. of Alinot; v. Allnutt.

headwords.meaning: doubtless a modification of Aglionby, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: The surname is found in Cumberland, and the full title was cumbrous.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Allen, q.v.; (2) de Alençon, in Normandy
headwords.author_comment: (2) Probably in some cases this is the true solution.

headwords.meaning: of Allerton, a parish five miles from Knaresborough, co. York; also a township in the parish of Childwall, near Liverpool; also a township in the parish of Kippax, W. Rid. York
headwords.author_comment: cf. Northallerton.

headwords.meaning: (1) of the Alley, i.e. from residence in a narrow passage; M.E. aley and alley; (2) probably in some cases Alley, a pet-name for Allen and Alice
headwords.author_comment: The first instance I possess is that of a foundling, found in an alley. But the name was an older one, of similar but more legitimate descent. The Hundred Rolls instances from Oxford and Cambridge seem very natural, just where we should expect alleys to be found; v. Twitchen. (2) A pet-name for very great favourites, Allen and Alice, q.v.; cf. Charlie, Teddy, &c.

headwords.meaning: see Alfrey
the son of Algod, a forgotten personal name
headwords.author_comment: Allgood, like Thoroughgood and Toogood, seems very complimentary, but it is without doubt a baptismal name, as are they. I see Lower says Algod occurs as a personal name before Domesday (Patr. Brit. p. 6).

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban, or Albon
headwords.author_comment: v. Allbon. The i and a are intrusive for euphony, as in Greenaway, Hathaway, for Greenway and Hathway; cf. Ottaway for Ottway. The d in Allibond is excrescent; cf. provincial gownd for gown, and v. Simmonds. A book on the 'Cure of Consumption' is advertized by the author, Edwin W. Alabone, in the Weekly Pulpit for May 22, 1887. Allaband and Alleborn are American variants.

headwords.meaning: of Allingham, a parish in co. Kent
of Allington, parishes in cos. Dorset, Kent, Wilts, Devon, and Lincoln
the son of Alice
headwords.author_comment: v. Alison (1).

headwords.meaning: variant of Alison
the son of Allen, from the dim. Allikin or Allkin
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Per-kin, Wat-kin, &c. Mr. Lower suggests that it stands for Halkin, the dim. of Henry. This view is defeated by the fact that Alkin has always been without the aspirate, and has always run side by side with its close relation Alcock, q.v. Let it not be forgotten that Allen, as one of the favourite personal names of the 13th and 14th centuries, must have had its popular nick. and pet forms. I have included Allchin and Alchin as variants of Allkin. But v. Allcorn.

headwords.meaning: the Alemaund, i.e. German; or still more locally 'of Alemaigne,' i.e. Germany
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Fr. Lallimond; cf. Fr. D'Almaine. With Almond cf. almond-furnace, i.e. a German furnace (H.E.D.); also under Almain, 'the almond-leape,' a German dance. 'The Almains ben ouer come,' 1314: Guy Warw. 70 (H.E.D.). 'Forth he went into Speyne And after into Almayne.'—ibid. 35. 'Item, the last daie (Nov. 1531) paide in rewarde to a gentleman of Almayne': Privy Purse Exp., Henry VIII, p. 178.

headwords.meaning: variant of Hallmark
the son of Alnot or Alnoth, the A.S. Alnod
headwords.author_comment: As will be seen from the above instances, Alnot or Alnoth remained in use as a personal name till the 16th century.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alot; query, a form of Eliot, with Eliota as fem.
headwords.author_comment: v. Elliot. In the Ulverston Registers, co. Lanc., the forms are Alletson, Aletson, Elatson, Elattson, Elletson, Eletson, all representing the same patronymic Eliotson; v. Alletson in Index of Registers of St. Mary, Ulverston. In any case the surname, with its variants, is of fontal origin.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldwy
headwords.author_comment: v. Allaway and Allvey, where Alway is clearly identified. From Alway or Allway to Alloway is an easy gradation; cf. Ottaway or Greenaway for Otway and Greenway. Alloway has ramified somewhat strongly in America. But it arose in England. No connexion with local Holloway; v. Allaway.

headwords.meaning: (?) the holy priest (?); A.S. halig, holy, from hal, whole
headwords.author_comment: Whatever the meaning, the following entry refers to the ancestor. Thus -prest (priest) and not -press is the suffix. The surname has always had cos. Cambridge and Hants for its habitat. There need be no anxiety as to the want of an h if Holy-priest be the parent. The Hundred Rolls (1273) in scores of cases ignore the aspirate. The Cockney is not in it, judging by early registers.

headwords.meaning: of Alsop-en-le-dale, a chapelry in the parish of Ashbourne, co. Derby
headwords.author_comment: The corruption 'Allsup' is suggestive of universal pale ale! The reason why Alsop and its variants are common in the United States is because several of the name were among the earliest settlers there.

headwords.meaning: variant of Alfred
the son of Aldwy, a fontal or personal name long ago forgotten in England
headwords.author_comment: It lives to-day in several patronymics. Of some land in Somerton, co. Norfolk, it is said 'the Conqueror had granted this to Alwy de Tetford' (FF. xi. 197).

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldrich
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower suggests Awl-wright, a maker of awls. The origin is obvious enough. It is a mere corruption of Alderich (now Aldrich and Aldridge, q.v.), thus: Alderich, Alrick, Alwright; cf. Woolwright for Wulfric (v. Woolrich), and Kenwright for Kendrick. A good example of the intermediate form is found in the following instances.

headwords.meaning: variant of Allman
(?) origin queried by the author
the Alpe, i.e. a bullfinch
headwords.author_comment: 'Alpe, a bryde: ficedula': Prompt. Parv. 'Alpes, fynches, and wodewales': Chaucer, R. R. 658. Alpe has existed as a surname in co. Norfolk for six centuries; cf. Finch, Sparrow, Nightingale, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Alstead
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the precise locality; but v. Halstead.

headwords.meaning: of Alston, a parish in co. Cumberland; a chapelry in the parish of Ashburton, co. Devon; a township in the parish of Ribchester, co. Lanc., &c. Also Alstone, a hamlet in the suburbs of Cheltenham, and a chapelry in the parish of Overbury, co. Worc.
possibly from the high and low range of voice
headwords.author_comment: But see legal 'alto et basso,' the submission of all differences, high and low, to an adjudicator (Bailey's Dict., 1742).

headwords.meaning: the ambler, one who looked after the amblers in his lord's stables; one who taught horses to amble
headwords.author_comment: Lower says 'le Ambleur, Fr., an officer of the king's stable.' Almost akin to Palfreyman, q.v. This surname has ramified strongly in Yorkshire. 'And mony fat palfray amblant' [i.e. ambling]. King Alisaunder, 3461. 'Upon an ambler esily she sat.' Chaucer, C. T. 471. Among his other duties the ambler broke in horses, i.e. taught them to amble. '1320. Item, pro informatione unius pulli ad ambulandum, 11s. 6d,' i.e. for teaching a colt to amble. Whittaker's Craven, p. 466.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 5; West Riding Court Dir., 25; Philadelphia, 18

headwords.meaning: the son of Amery
headwords.author_comment: q.v.; cf. Emberson and Embery from Emery. The b is intrusive, as usual after m.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ambrose; Fr. Ambroise
headwords.author_comment: No doubt the fair amount of popularity obtained in England for this fontal name was due to the great St. Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan. The Church would not readily let his name be lost in obscurity (v. Yonge, Hist. Christian Names, i. 248). Ambrosi is a familiar Italian surname.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amy, from the double dim. Amel-ot
headwords.author_comment: (v. Ames and Amyot); cf. Hamelot from Hamo, or Hewel-ot from Hugh or Hew; v. Hamlet and Hewlett.

headwords.meaning: the son of Meredith, Ap-Meredith
headwords.author_comment: Lower speaks of this name as still existing.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amery or Emery
headwords.author_comment: q.v.; common to both sexes. Other variants were Americ, Almeric, and Almaric. It was decidedly popular. In the Italian dress of Amerigo it gave title to the great western continent. The United States has restored the feminine form in America, not an uncommon font-name for girls. I see in the Boston Directory, 'America Anderson, widow.' However strangely this may read, it was a common girl's name six centuries ago.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amys, or the son of Amy, with the patronymic s
headwords.author_comment: 'Amye, Amy, propre name: Amia': Prompt. Parv. The origin is the same. But Amice or Amys seems to have become the popular English form of the O.F. Aimée, just as Piers or Pearce came to represent the O.F. Pierre. Perhaps the Latinized forms had something to do with it. The two first entries occur close together, and probably refer to the same individual. Amia, Amicia, Amise, and Amisius all occur as personal names without surnames in the Hundred Rolls, 1273. The form Amiss in the London Directory is met by the entry 'Gregory Amys, or Amisse'. In the United States the form is all but invariably Ames. Amice or Ames continued as a girl's fontal name till the 16th century. The family of Ames in the Register of St. Dionis Backchurch is found as Amyes (p. 8), 1576; Ames and Ammes (p. 130), 1690; and Amis (p. 22), 1627. In the Register of St. Michael, Cornhill, the name is often found as Aymes.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amflis
headwords.author_comment: This name seems to be extinct. It has long been forgotten as a fontal name, and so far I can find the surname no later than the 16th century.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amabel
headwords.author_comment: v. Annable and Hanniball.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Amias (v. Ames); (2) of Amiens
the son of Amice; v. Ames
headwords.author_comment: The Amsons of co. Ches. all descend from Ameson.

headwords.meaning: the amner, i.e. almoner, a distributor of alms in a religious house or household
headwords.author_comment: 'Was Jesu Crist ammoner?' 1300, Cursor Mundi, 15219. 'Dr Fox the Kynges Amner made an eloquent oracion in Latin': 1548, Hall, Chron. 790 (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: at the Moor
headwords.author_comment: Abbreviated to A'Moor; cf. A'Beckett, Abrook, A'Wood, &c.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amys
headwords.author_comment: Without doubt a variant, and one more instance of the great popularity of Amice. The name of the Old Test. prophet was unknown in the 13th century. There is not a single trace of its existence. Amos, like Amias or Amyas, represents popular forms of the Norman-French Aimée, or Amys, now generally known as Amy; v. Ames. I do not suppose there were any Amos's previous to the Reformation. This variant has arisen since the Bible, in the vulgar tongue, became familiar to the people. It is simply imitative. The above Aaron Amos may have been a Jew.

headwords.meaning: of Amfleet
headwords.author_comment: One of many local names found on the east coast of England, from Durham to Suffolk, which have -fleet for their suffix, a shallow creek. I have not yet identified the place. [Since writing the above I find my statement as to suffix confirmed, but not that relating to the locality. Mr. Lower quotes Lambarde's Dictionary: 'Amflete, Amfleot, et aliis Ampleot, a haven in France, as I gesse, near Boloigne'; v. Patr. Brit. p. 8.]

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Ampe
headwords.author_comment: This has been a Cambridgeshire surname for six centuries. It is possible that it is of local origin, but there is no local prefix in my references from the Hundred Rolls, and the patronymic form Amps (cf. Williams, Jones, Wilkins, &c.) is confirmatory proof.

headwords.meaning: the son of Amiot, from Amy, O.F. Amé or Aimée, dim. Ami-ot
headwords.author_comment: We find Aimée in north England at an early period in the entry: Amya del Stable, 1379. Cf. also Ammya de Wydecombe.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Ancel, whence dims. Ancelot and Ancelin (v. Lancelot and Lancelin); (2) the son of Anselm (?)
headwords.author_comment: I merely suggest this as a possibility. No doubt the final m in Anselm might be easily dropped. But of course (1) is the true and natural solution in the majority of cases.

headwords.meaning: the son of John, a variant of Hancock
headwords.author_comment: A vile variant of Hancock, q.v.; cf. the common United States surname, Arrison. It is interesting to note that Ancock is found in the county which had so close a connexion with the Flemings, who introduced Han, Hans, &c. Annis represents Agnes; v. Annis.

headwords.meaning: the son of Andrew
headwords.author_comment: q.v. It was of course inevitable that Andrewson should become toned down to Anderson. Even Andrews has occasionally assumed the form of Anders.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Anderton, a township in the parish of Standish, co. Lanc.; (2) of Anderton, a township in the parish of Great Budworth, co. Chester
headwords.author_comment: There seems to be a second Anderton. Samuel Oldknow, of Mellor, was 'born at Anderton, near Bolton, in Lancashire, Oct. 5, 1756, ... and established a large muslin manufactory at Stockport in 1784': v. East Cheshire, ii. 54. Probably, however, the same place is meant.

headwords.meaning: the son of Andrew; v. Anderson
headwords.author_comment: This name was very popular in the 13th century. As the name of the patron saint and knightly champion of Scotland, as title of the primatial see, no wonder that the Scotch have tried to monopolize Andrew, and no wonder that Anderson has followed Scotch emigration till Canada and the United States are flooded with it. But Andrew was very popular in its day in England, as our Andrews can testify. In any case, as an apostolic name it was bound to be popular all over Europe.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Angel; in later days Angela and Angelina; (2) at the Angle; v. Angle
headwords.author_comment: For the full history of this once-popular name, v. Yonge, i. 126-7. The Puritans could not oust this name, though bitterly hated by them. (2) Most probably the source of the majority of our Angels and Angells. The font-name was unknown in England, so far as I can discover, in the 13th and 14th centuries.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Aunger; (2) of Angers, a city of Anjou
headwords.author_comment: (1) This is the probable origin of most of the variants found in modern directories.

headwords.meaning: in the Angle, i.e. nook, corner; from residence in some nook or corner of the road
headwords.author_comment: 'Go, run, search, pry in every nook and angle of the kitchens, larders, and pastries': The Woman Hater, i. 2; v. Nangle, and cf. Herne and Wray. The English portion of the Angels and Angells in the London Directory are probably from this source; v. Angel.

headwords.meaning: the son of Angold or Angod
of Angus, N.B.
headwords.author_comment: Although most of the instances occur in co. Norfolk, it will be seen that they are of comparatively modern date. They represent an immigration from the north. There can be no doubt about the origin. It is simply imitative, as was the custom in spelling or even pronouncing surnames.

headwords.meaning: the Angevine, an immigrant from Anjou
headwords.author_comment: Although fairly common in mediaeval registers, this surname barely survives. It has obtained a footing, however, in the United States.

headwords.meaning: the anker, an anchorite or hermit; see Ankerman
headwords.author_comment: 'Sometime I am religious, Now like an anker in an hous': Chaucer, R. R. 6348. The following is imitative, the second instance probably being the name of a foundling, discovered at an inn styled 'the Anchor.'

headwords.meaning: the ankerman, i.e. the servant of the anker or hermit
headwords.author_comment: now generally styled an anchorite; but ancre was the earlier form. Cf. Matthewman, Monkman, Priestman, Vikerman, Armetman (v. Armet), &c., all Yorkshire surnames. 'An anchor's cheer in prison be my scope': Hamlet, iii. 2. My one London Directory instance deserves to be set in full: 'Frederic Ankerman, boot-maker, 77, Provost St., Hoxton.' Probably u is a misreading for n in the following entries [Aukereswoman]. Cotgrave has ankrosse, a female hermit.

headwords.meaning: the son of Arnketel, eagle cauldron
headwords.author_comment: Arkettle, q.v., is but another form of the same name. Both are compounds of 'Kettle,' q.v. The Norman form was Anskettle; v. Oskettle. I dare not say this surname is extinct in England, for I find one in Crockford; see, however, Anskettle and Arkettle.

headwords.meaning: the son of Annable, a corruption of Amable; v. Hanniball
headwords.author_comment: This surname is well represented in the United States.

headwords.meaning: of Annan or Annandale, a parish and dale in co. Dumfries, through which the river Annan flows
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Simmonds for Simmons, or the provincial gownd for gown.

headwords.headword: Annis, Annison, Anningson, Anness, Aningson, Annin, Anning
headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Ann, from the dim. Annie; (2) the son of Agnes, popularly Annis, Annes, or Annas
headwords.author_comment: 'Pay me, quod he, or by the swete Seinte Anne': Chaucer, C. T. 7193. The variant Anningson is curious, and seems founded upon some early dim. Annin, with an excrescent g, as in Jennings; cf. Pattison and Pattinson. In general (2) must be looked upon as the parent of all these names. Annis was the popular form of Agnes from the 14th century downwards. 'Annys: propyr name (Anneys, H., Annyce, P.)—Agnes': Prompt. Parv. [Of Anish Luke, Annis Thring, Annise Teswell and Annis Brittanie:] All these cases are feminine, and represent Agnes.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0; MDB. (Norfolk), 0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0; (Lincoln), 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0; (Burnley, co. Lanc.) Anningson, 1; Philadelphia, 3, 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1

headwords.meaning: the son of Alianore, popularly Annore, whence later Nora, or Norah
the son of Anne, dim. Ann-ot; v. Anson for many instances and fuller history
headwords.author_comment: 'Annet, the common gull, so called in Northumberland': Halliwell. No doubt taken from the once popular dim. of Anne, especially popular on the north-east coast of England. Annot Alyface is a character in Ralph Roister Doister, by Nicholas Udall, written about 1550, where she sings 'Work, Tibet: work, Annot: work, Margery ...': Dodsley's Old English Plays, iii. 72.

headwords.meaning: variant of Ancell
the son of Anselm
headwords.author_comment: This personal name was decidedly popular in its day, and if it has no representatives in our modern directories, the explanation is simple: they have become incorporated with our Ansells; v. Ancell.

headwords.headword: Anskettle, Askettle, Askell, Askill, Aiskell, Askel
headwords.meaning: the son of Anskettle, or Askettle, or Askell (kettle as a suffix always became kell, kill, or kle)
headwords.author_comment: Anskettle (a variant of Oskettle, q.v.) was probably a Norman introduction. For other instances, v. Astell.

headwords.meaning: the son of Anne; v. Annis and Annott

headwords.headword: Anstee, Anstey, Anstie, Ansty, Anstice, Anstise, Anstiss
headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Anastasia, from the nick. Anstie and Anstice; (2) of Anstey or Ansty, parishes in diocese of Peterborough, Sarum, St. Albans, Exeter, and Worcester
headwords.author_comment: 'Anstiss, Anstish, Anstyce, all occur frequently as female names in the older pages of a Devonshire parish, where Anstice is now a surname': Yonge, i. 250. (2) This will concern Anstey, Anstie, and Ansty only. Anstice, Anstis, and Anstiss are undoubtedly to be placed under (1).

headwords.meaning: of Anstruther, in co. Fife, N.B.
headwords.author_comment: 'William de Candela held the barony of Anstruther, in co. Fife, about 1153. His grandson Henry appears to have assumed the surname in or before 1221' (Lower).

headwords.meaning: the son of Antony; the h is intrusive
headwords.author_comment: 'Antony, propyr name, Antonius': Prompt. Parv. The name had become fairly popular in England in the 13th century, as having been borne by the great hermit of the 4th century. He was the patron saint of the swineherd, and 'as fat as a Tantony pig,' and 'to follow like a Tantony pig,' became proverbial expressions; v. Yonge, i. 306; Halliwell, i. 67. 'I have behest a pygge to Saynt Antony'; v. Prompt. Parv. p. 29, and note by Way.

headwords.meaning: of Ampthill
headwords.author_comment: I owe the suggestion to Lower, and doubt not it is correct. The corruption was inevitable. Cf. Amphield, or Anfield, a hamlet in the parish of Hursley. Ampthill is a market town seven miles from Bedford. The surname in its corrupted form is better represented in the United States than in England. A single glance at the two forms below will settle any doubts as to the true parentage of the name. The second entry practically settles any doubt.

headwords.meaning: of Antioch
headwords.author_comment: cf. Veness, Janeway, &c. Probably imported as the result of the spicery trade with the East. I cannot discover any modern representatives.

headwords.meaning: of Arncliff, a village and parish, W. Rid. of Yorkshire, sixteen miles north of Shipton
headwords.author_comment: In local names, whose suffix is -cliff, there is a tendency to elide the c; cf. Cunliffe or Topliff for Cuncliff and Topcliff. This surname has crossed the Atlantic. No doubt the meaning is the eagle-cliff.

headwords.meaning: the son of Antony; Fr. Antoine, Ger. Anton, M.E. Antoyn
headwords.author_comment: Of course many of the United States representatives are of French and German extraction.

headwords.meaning: of Antrobus, a township in the parish of Great Budworth, co. Cheshire
headwords.author_comment: Apart from the well-known family of that name and place, many Antrobus's may be seen in the Lanc. and Cheshire directories. They may represent junior branches of centuries ago or separate stocks. This surname has crossed the Atlantic.

headwords.meaning: of Anvers, i.e. Antwerp
headwords.author_comment: This surname seemingly did not last long. I find no representatives during the last three centuries.

headwords.meaning: the son of Anwyl
headwords.author_comment: This is a Welsh surname, and as at least ninety-five per cent. of its nomenclature is baptismal, I feel bound to place it under that class; but I have not met with the name in early records.
headwords.modern_distribution: MDB. (co. Montgomery), 2, 0; (co. Denbigh), 1, 0; (co. Flint), 1, 0; (co. Carnarvon), 1, 0; London, 1, 0; Liverpool, 1, 1; Philadelphia, 2, 0

headwords.meaning: the son of Eignion or Enion, a Welsh surname; v. Benyon and Eynon
the ape
headwords.author_comment: For a reason that can be well understood this surname has not come down to modern times. 'Wilde beris and apes,' 1350: Will. Palerne, 2298 (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Appoline; (2) the son of Abel, from dim. Abelin, sharpened to Apelin; (3) the son of Lyon, a Welsh personal name, whence the patr. ap-Lyon
headwords.author_comment: The homily 'Against the perils of Idolatry' says, 'All diseases have their special saints as gods, the curers of them: the toothache, St. Appoline.' This was the usual English form of Appolonia, a martyr at Alexandria, who, among other tortures, had all her teeth beaten out. It was a popular girl's name, and survived the Reformation. (2) cf. Apps for Abbs, or Epps for Ebbs. (3) This undoubtedly became Applin, and represents the Applins of cos. Somerset, Hereford, and south-west England generally; cf. Applejohn.

headwords.meaning: of Apperley: (1) an extra-parochial district in the parish of Bywell, co. Northumberland; (2) a hamlet in the parish of Deerhurst, co. Glouc., near Tewkesbury
headwords.author_comment: The above entries seem to prove that Apperley, in co. Glouc., is the real parent.

headwords.meaning: of Appleby, parishes in cos. Westmoreland, Lincoln, and Leicester
headwords.author_comment: Many local surnames ending in by are now found as bee, as this dictionary proves in various pages.

headwords.meaning: of Appledore; parishes in the dioceses of Canterbury and Exeter
of Appleford, a chapelry in the parish of Sutton Courtney, co. Berks
of the Apple-garth, apple, and garth, an enclosure (an orchard); v. Appleyard
headwords.author_comment: 'Appelle-garth: pometum': Cath. Angl. This surname seems now generally found as Applegate. [After the citations:] This last is a second entry of a name instanced above.

headwords.meaning: a seller of apples
headwords.author_comment: Cf. 'apple-monger: pomilius': Huloet, 1552.

headwords.meaning: of Applethwaite, a township in the parish of Windermere, co. Westmoreland
headwords.author_comment: With Applewhite, cf. Hebblewhite for Hebblethwaite.

headwords.meaning: of Appleton; parishes in the dioceses of Norwich, Oxford, York (3), and Ripon. From appel or appil, apple, and ton, a town, an enclosure
headwords.author_comment: The meaning is obvious: appel or appil, apple, and ton, a town, an enclosure; cf. Appleyard and Applegarth. Many places would naturally acquire such a title. There are townships so called in cos. Lancaster and Chester.

headwords.meaning: (1) at the apple-tree; (2) of Appletree, a hamlet in co. Northampton, seven miles from Banbury
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Plumptree, Rowntree, Crabtree, &c. Of course the origin is the same.

headwords.meaning: of the Appleyard, from apple, and yard, or garth, an enclosure, an orchard
headwords.author_comment: 'Appullyerde, or gardeyne, or orcherde: Pomerium': Prompt. Parv. Evidently a familiar word all over the kingdom for an orchard; cf. Applegarth.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 8; West Riding Court Dir., 16; Boston (U.S.), 2

headwords.meaning: see Aplin
the son of Abraham, or Abel, from the nick. Abb, sharpened to App
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Epps for Ebbs, Hopkins for Hobkins, Hopps for Hobbs, &c. But it is only fair to suggest that App may have been the nick. for the 13th century popular name of Apsalon (Absolom). Apps would then be the patronymic. I have no evidence for this, and merely throw it out for consideration. There can be no doubt that if Apsalon be cast aside, then Apps stands for Abbs, q.v. Since writing the above I have come across the following entry: [Thomas atte Apse] This, of course, is a local surname, and may share in the parentage of Apps. This would be by residence beside the apse of a church; cf. Galilee, Porch, &c.

headwords.meaning: a corruption of Harbottle, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Found, like Harbottle, in the neighbourhood of that place. This surname has crossed the Atlantic, and is spreading in the United States.

headwords.meaning: of Arbuthnot, a parish in Kincardineshire
headwords.author_comment: 'a parish in Kincardineshire. The first of the family was Hugh de Arburbothenoth, who assumed his surname from the lands which he acquired in 1105 with the daughter of Osbert Olifard, and on which his descendants have resided for more than twenty generations': Lower's Pat. Brit. p. 10.

headwords.meaning: a corruption of Archibald, q.v.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 1; New York, 1

headwords.meaning: a great braggart
headwords.author_comment: Arch = chief, as in Archdeacon, Archpriest, q.v. Also cf. 'archewives': Chaucer, C. T. 9071.

headwords.meaning: the son of Archibald
headwords.author_comment: These three are simply variants; v. Archibald.

headwords.meaning: the archdeacon
headwords.author_comment: The name still survives, and not long ago I saw it over a hatter's shop. 'Daniel Archdeacon was recommended to the king for his services, 1610': State Papers, 1623-5, p. 545. Quite recently some members of the Archdeacon family have adopted the mediaeval Arcedekne, 'not wisely, but too well.'
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 0; Halifax, 1, 0; Liverpool, 2, 0; MDB. (co. Norfolk), 0, 1; Boston (U.S.), 5, 0

headwords.meaning: the archer, a professional bowman; O.F. archier
headwords.author_comment: The arbalester was a cross-bowman; v. Alabaster; cf. Bowman, Bowmaker, Fletcher, Flower, &c.

headwords.meaning: variant of Aitcheson; not the son of the Archer
the son of Archibald; German, Erchanbald; O.F. Archambault; Italian, Arcibaldo
headwords.author_comment: Miss Yonge (ii. 255) adds, 'So frequent was it (Archibald) in the houses of Campbell and Douglas, that, with its contractions of Archie and Baldie, it has become one of the most commonly used in Scotland, recalling many a fierce worthy, from old Archibald Bell-the-Cat downwards.' Archbold, Archbutt, and Archbould are modern English forms of the surname; v. Archbold, Archbutt. Archambault is common in Philadelphia. Twelve representatives appear in the directory. This is the result of French immigration.

headwords.meaning: the archpriest, a chief priest, a vicar to a bishop, later a rural dean
headwords.author_comment: V. H.E.D. The term was in use in the 17th century, for Smith, the 'silver-tongued' preacher, speaks of 'priest, or priests, or archpriests, or any such like': God's Arrow against Atheists.

headwords.meaning: of Arderne
headwords.author_comment: The present representatives in south-east Lanc. directories preserve the spellings, as Arden and Ardren are frequently found in the records of the family. They resided at Harden Hall, near Stockport, and are reputed to have been an early branch of the Warwickshire Ardernes; v. East Cheshire, i. 161. The de was dropped about 1420.

headwords.meaning: of or from Argentan, a town in south Normandy
headwords.author_comment: David de Argentomago was a tenant-in-chief under the Conqueror in cos. Bedford and Camb. His descendants were ennobled as Barons Argentine (Lower).

headwords.meaning: of Arras, a town in Artois famous for the manufacture of tapestry
headwords.author_comment: Not a vulgarism for Harris. [Quotations illustrating 'arras': 1536. 'Claithis of arres and tapestreis': Bellendene, Cron. Scotl. ii. 56 (H.E.D.). 1562. 'One bede coveringe of aries worke, 8s': Richmondshire Wills, i. 161.]

headwords.meaning: the son of Arketel
headwords.author_comment: Norsk, Arnkjell, eagle cauldron; v. Yonge, ii. 283. One more compound of Kettle (q.v.) contracted to kell, kill, or kle. 'Archill revolts against William': Freeman, Norman Conquest, iv. 186.

headwords.meaning: variant of Artingstall
a maker of arks; v. Arkwright
the arkwright, a maker of arks
headwords.author_comment: This article of furniture was a north English manufacture, and the surname originated there. The ark was the old-fashioned meal-chest. 'When this corn to the kniht was sold, He did it in an arc to hold, And opened this arc the third day': Tale of a Usurer. In an inventory of household goods, dated 1559, are mentioned 'one trussin bed, with a teaster of yealow and chamlet, one old arke, old hanggers, of wull grene and red,' &c.: Richmondshire Wills, p. 135. Twenty years earlier I find the contents of a 'mylke howse' including 'an arke, a tub, a stande, a chyrne': ibid. p. 42. In the same book a sheep is bequeathed to one Henry Arkwright, p. 155, note.

headwords.meaning: for Harlot, a fellow, a servant
headwords.author_comment: 'A sturdy harlot wente hem ay behind': Chaucer, C. T. 7336. 'He was a gentil harlot, and a kind': ibid. 649. Professor Skeat connects Charlotte with this word, and refers to Arletta, the reputed mother of William I; v. Harlot (Skeat's Dict.).

headwords.meaning: the son of Armund
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Rayment for Raymund, or Garment for Garmund. The true English form is Armine or Armyn; Fr. Armand; Dutch, Herman.

headwords.meaning: the armourer, a maker of armour
headwords.author_comment: 'Armurers and Arowsmythis,' c. 1400: Destr. Troy, v. 1588 (H.E.D.). 'Armateur, an Armer, a provider of armes or weapons': Cotgrave (H.E.D.).

headwords.meaning: armiger, an armour-bearer, a squire
headwords.author_comment: This became Arminger, just as Potager became Pottinger, and Messager Messinger. Thus n is intrusive.

headwords.meaning: the son of Armand; v. Arment
headwords.author_comment: Armandson would easily vary to Arminson, and this to Armson.

headwords.meaning: at the Hermitstead, from residence at a hermitage or hermit-stead
headwords.author_comment: M.E. eremite, a hermit, pronounced armit; cf. Clark and Clerk, Darby and Derby, &c. This has been a Yorkshire surname for five centuries at least; see next article.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Rid. Court Dir., 6, 1, 1; London, 4, 2, 1; Philadelphia, 2, 0, 0; Boston (U.S.), 0, 6, 0

headwords.meaning: the hermit
headwords.author_comment: M.E. eremite and heremite. Pronounced also armit as in Armitage (q.v.) for Hermitage; see last article.

headwords.meaning: of the Hermitage
headwords.author_comment: Once pronounced harmitage or armitage in the north; cf. Clerk and Clark, Derby and Darby, &c.; v. Armit and Armistead. A great Lancashire and Yorkshire surname.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 56, 0; London, 12, 3; Philadelphia, 17, 0

headwords.meaning: variant of Ormerod
headwords.author_comment: An American variant.

headwords.meaning: arm-strong; cf. Strongitharm
headwords.author_comment: The name of a familiar Border clan. 'Ye need not go to Liddisdale, For when they see the blazing bale Elliots and Armstrongs never fail.' This surname has ramified very strongly in the States and in Canada.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Arnold; (2) of Arnold, a village in the parish of Long Riston, co. York; also of Arnold, a parish in co. Notts
headwords.author_comment: The omission of the final d in Arnald was perfectly natural, just as natural as to have added it if it were not there; cf. provincial gownd for gown, or Simmonds for Simmons.

headwords.meaning: the son of Arne, either the nick. of Arnold (v. Arnett) or a personal name Arn (eagle), which is itself the first syllable of Arnold
the son of Arnold; v. Arnold and Arnott
headwords.author_comment: An early corruption.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Arnold, through some nick. or pet form; v. Arnold; (2) the son of Arnys; v. Harness
headwords.author_comment: Armeson may be a corruption. Arnoldson, which exists to-day in the United States, would naturally become Arnison; see next article for instances in the Hundred Rolls.

headwords.meaning: the son of Arnold; Fr. Arnoud
headwords.author_comment: With the corruption Arnott, cf. Archbutt for Archibald. Of course Arnold is now practically forgotten as a personal name in England. Nevertheless it was very popular in its day, and being in great favour just when fontal names were candidates for immortality as surnames, it is not to be wondered at that Arnold and its variants and corruptions are familiar to all our directories at the close of the 19th century. I only furnish a few instances. The United States has such continental forms as Arnhold and Arnholt.

headwords.meaning: the son of Arnulf; v. Arnolf, Yonge, ii. 282
headwords.author_comment: Just as Randolph or Randulf became Randle, so Arnulf, no doubt, became Arnull, and thus was lost in Arnell and other variants of Arnold, q.v.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aaron
headwords.author_comment: Generally of Jewish descent, but not necessarily so in all cases. From Aran to Arran was an easy transition. This, with an excrescent d, became Arrend; cf. gownd for gown, or Simmonds for Simmons. There can be no doubt about the fact that Arrend is Aaron in disguise.

headwords.meaning: the son of Harry (v. Harrison)
headwords.author_comment: Unless Arrison be a corruption of Aaronson, which is not probable. I fear there are Cockneys in America as well as in London.

headwords.meaning: the arrowsmith, a maker of iron tips, a smith
headwords.author_comment: This surname is corrupted to Athersmith in Furness, North Lanc. I have two Athersmiths in my parish (Ulverston). A late occupative term. No instance in the Hundred Rolls or any other records of the 13th century, so far as my researches go. For the earliest instance given in the H.E.D. (c. 1400) v. Armer. 'Arowe-heders, maltemen, and corn mongers.' 1510. Cocke Lorelles Bote.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ancelot; v. Ancell and Lancelot
headwords.author_comment: There can be little doubt about this solution, but I have no absolute proof. If Ancelot was known familiarly as Ascelot, then the rest is easy to accept.

headwords.meaning: the son of Arthur
headwords.author_comment: A rare font-name in the Hundred Rolls. Very common since the battle of Waterloo and the publication of Tennyson's poems.

headwords.meaning: of Artinstall
headwords.author_comment: I do not know the precise spot, nor can I say whether it is in Lancashire or Cheshire. The following entries will assist in the search. One thing is certain, Arstill and Artinstall represent the same name.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Arthur, a corruption of Arthurs or Arters; v. Arthur; (2) of Artois
headwords.author_comment: The final s will thus be patronymic, as in Williams, Jones, Jennings, Wilkins, &c. The two first (not Artson) might easily be so derived. But I have no instances.

headwords.meaning: of Arundel, a parish in dioc. of Chichester, co. Sussex, ten miles from Chichester
the son of Asculf
headwords.author_comment: No doubt this surname is lost in Hasell and Hazell, q.v. There are no modern representatives of the true original form. Probably some of the many Hasells and Hazells of Berkshire (a district which was familiar with the fontal name Asculf or Hascul) are to be referred to this source.

headwords.meaning: v. Hasleden; an American variant
at the ash, from the original bearer's residence by a certain ash-tree
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birch, Oak, Lynde, and v. Nash. 'Esche-tre - fraxinus': Prompt. Parv. p. 143.

headwords.meaning: of Ashbourne, a well-known parish in co. Derby
the ash-burner
headwords.author_comment: One of the oldest and most familiar names in Furness and the English Lake district. The ash-burner was a manufacturer of charcoal, to be used for the bloom-smithies of the middle ages. It is probable that the ash-burner's craft covered the process of smelting as well. The traces of ancient bloomeries are still to be found in the coppice woods that skirt the shores of Windermere, Coniston, and the Duddon estuary. Gradually the occupative term became collier, and ousted the other. The surname, Ashburner, however, will for ever remain a memorial of the primitive period when iron ore was smelted in the woods, whose trees supplied the fuel; see Bloomer and Collier. Instances from the Furness church registers are needless; they abound on every page.

headwords.meaning: of Ashby, parishes in diocs. of Lincoln (4), Norwich (3), Peterborough (7)
headwords.author_comment: With Ashbee, cf. Applebee.

headwords.meaning: of Ashcroft; i.e. the croft or enclosure where the ash-trees grew
headwords.author_comment: Seemingly a Norfolk surname. The suffix -croft is often found as -craft; cf. Meadowcroft and Meadowcraft, and v. Croft and Craft, or Crofter and Crafter. Of course the origin is simple enough, i.e. the croft or enclosure where the ash-trees grew. It is quite clear also that a Lancashire family are sprung from a place named Ashcroft in that county.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Ashdown, a parish in dioc. of Chichester; (2) of Ashdon, a parish in co. Essex, three miles from Saffron Walden
of Ashenden, a parish in dioc. of Oxford, co. Bucks
variant of Asser
of Ashfield, two parishes in co. Suffolk and a township in co. Salop
of Ashford, parishes in diocs. of Canterbury, Exeter, London, Southwell, and Hereford
headwords.author_comment: v. Ford and Forth for the two suffixes.

headwords.meaning: of Ashley, parishes in diocs. of Canterbury, Chester, Ely, Gloucester and Bristol, Lichfield, Peterborough, Winchester, and Oxford
variant of Aslin
the son of Ashman
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bateman. This surname would seem at first sight to be local, representing one who lived at the ash-tree (v. Ash and Nash), but there can be little doubt that it is a personal name, and perchance the same as Assemannus in Domesday; cf. the place-names Ashmanhaugh, Ashmansworth, compounded with the name of the original tenant. Cf. the German surname Aschemann; one occurs in the New York Directory.

headwords.meaning: of Ashmead, i.e. some spot where the mead or meadow was surrounded by ash-trees
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot. The surname has ramified strongly in America.

headwords.meaning: of Ashmore, a parish in co. Dorset, five miles from Shaftesbury

of Ashton or Aston, parishes in diocs. of Exeter, Peterborough, Bath and Wells, Sarum, Gloucester and Bristol, Chester, Liverpool, and Manchester; the ash-town, i.e. the enclosure with ash-trees in it
headwords.author_comment: The meaning is simple: the ash-town, i.e. the enclosure with ash-trees in it; v. Ash and Town. Naturally this would be a common place-name. With the form Aston, cf. Ascroft and Ashcroft.

headwords.meaning: of Ashurst: (1) a parish in co. Kent, about four miles from Tunbridge Wells; (2) a parish in co. Sussex, three miles from Steyning; 'the Ash-hurst' or wood
headwords.author_comment: The origin is simple, 'the Ash-hurst' or wood; v. Ash and Hurst. There is evidently a spot in co. Lanc. bearing this name.

headwords.meaning: of Ashwell: (1) a parish in co. Hertford, about four miles from Baldock; (2) a parish in co. Rutland, three miles from Oakham
of Ashworth, a chapelry in the parish of Middleton, co. Lanc., anciently Asseheworth
headwords.author_comment: This small place (pop. 233 in 1861) has given birth to a surname that has become largely represented. It is familiar to every town and village in south Lancashire. Henry Ashworth (1794-1880), the friend of Cobden, was born at Birtwistle, near Bolton, a few miles from Ashworth, on Sept. 4, 1794. Caleb Ashworth, D.D. (1722-75), a celebrated dissenter, was born at Rossendale, co. Lanc. John Ashworth (1813-75), preacher, manufacturer, and author, was born at Cutgate, near Rochdale; v. Dict. Nat. Biog. ii. 187-8. The little village has kept itself well in the remembrance of Lancashire people.

headwords.meaning: of Aske, a township in the parish of Easby, near Richmond, North Riding of Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: This surname is nearly, but not quite, obsolete. 'Robert Aske (d. 1537), leader of the insurrection called the "Pilgrimage of Grace," was of an old Yorkshire family which took its name from Aske, in Richmondshire': v. Dict. Nat. Biog. ii. 189.

headwords.meaning: the son of Askettle; v. Anskettle
of Aiskew, a township in the parish of Bedale, co. York; v. Askey
headwords.author_comment: 'Anne Askew (1521-46), protesting martyr, was the second daughter of Sir William Askew, or Ayscough, knight, who is generally stated to be of Kelsey, in Lincolnshire': Dict. Nat. Biog. (v. Askew). As shown above, the original form was Aiskew or Ayscough. This by an intrusive n became, in Lancashire, Ainscough and Ainscow. But Askew is the generally adopted form. It was natural that the surname should cross the border from Yorkshire to Lancashire.

headwords.meaning: variant of Askew
headwords.author_comment: These are variants. It is perfectly natural to find Askey in co. Lincoln, where Askew was familiar for centuries.

headwords.meaning: of Askham, two parishes in co. York; also Askham, a parish in co. Cumb., near Barrow-in-Furness
headwords.author_comment: 'Roger Ascham (1515-68) was born in 1515 at Kirby Wiske, near Northallerton. His family seems to have been of considerable antiquity, and to have taken its name from the villages known as East and West Askham, near York. A Roger de Askham is mentioned as an adherent of Thomas, Earl of Lancaster, in 1313': Dict. Nat. Biog. ii. 150.

headwords.meaning: the son of Anskettle, q.v.
the son of Asketin (?), an O.F. dim. of Askettle
headwords.author_comment: As Askettle became undoubtedly Askell, q.v., so Asketin probably became Askin. For further instances and remarks, v. Astell. Nevertheless, I am not quite satisfied with this solution. Like Wilkin and Wilkins from William, it would appear that Askin and Askins represent a popular nick. of some once familiar personal name.

headwords.meaning: of Askwith, a village in the parish of Weston, near Otley, co. York
headwords.author_comment: Askwith and Ashworth are the same compound, viz. Ash and Worth, q.v. Asquith is the modern popular dress.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 0, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 3, 9; Philadelphia, 0, 5

headwords.meaning: the son of Aslak; v. Yonge, i. 46
headwords.author_comment: A well-known name in its time, of Scandinavian origin. Cf. the local Aslacton. These would signify 'the dwelling of Aslac.' The Rev. Oscar Aslachson occurs in Crockford, 1886.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ancel, from the dim. Ancelin, popularly Asselin or Acelin; v. Ancell
headwords.author_comment: Asselin and Ascelyne occur as personal names in the Hundred Rolls without surnames attached; v. Lancelin. The corruption to Ashlin is clearly traceable. The g in Asling is excrescent, as in Jennings, &c. The Cambridgeshire form is Ashling. Six centuries ago, in the same county, it was Asselin. But the change is an ordinary one.

headwords.meaning: of Aspden, a village near Buntingford, co. Hertford
headwords.author_comment: As nearly all the instances are found in Lancashire it is quite possible another locality exists, or has existed, in that county called Aspden. The origin of the word is simple; v. Dean and Aspinall.

headwords.meaning: of Aspall, a parish in co. Suffolk, one mile from Debenham
headwords.author_comment: Probably the Lancashire Aspells represent Aspinall, q.v.: a clear instance is there given. This surname has crossed the Atlantic. Oddly enough, I find but scanty English representatives as yet.

headwords.meaning: the son of Absolom (O.E. Aspelon)
headwords.author_comment: O.E. Aspelon. The change of b to p, and removal of s from after to before p, seem to have begun in the early decades of the 13th century. This font-name was very popular, and as a surname has existed in co. Cambridge for six centuries. The first three instances above are from the county of Cambridge. It is odd to think that Asplen is unquestionably from Absolom.

headwords.meaning: of Aspinwall, a property in the parish of Aughton, co. Lanc.; lit. 'the aspen-well', i.e. the poplar-well, the well by the poplar-trees
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Popplewell. We still speak of 'trembling like an aspen-leaf.' Were there the slightest doubt that Aspinall is a variant of Aspinwall, the above quotations would set the question at rest for ever. The place is styled Aspinall in documents, 15 Charles I; v. Exchequer Depositions by Commission, Lancashire (Lanc. and Ches. Record Soc. V. xi. 26).

headwords.meaning: see Aspenlon
of Askwith (v. Askwith)
the son of Asser
headwords.author_comment: 'Asser (says Mr. Lower), an ancient personal name, as Asserius Menevensis, the preceptor of King Alfred. Two tenants called Azor are found in Domesday': Patr. Brit. p. 13. The frequent occurrence of Asher in the United States directories is due to an influx of German Aschers, who perhaps represent the same personal name.

headwords.meaning: variant of Ashman (v. Ashman)
the son of Asketel
headwords.author_comment: One of the many corruptions of this early and popular name; v. Oskell. Asketel became, of course, Askil; v. Kell. Hence the Askils below. From Askil to Astell was an easy transition. Aschetil de Ousegarth, co. York, is set down in one record variously as Aschetin, Asketin, Aschetel, and Astill; v. Index, FFF. As Asketin was a familiar form (possibly diminutive) of Asketel, it is probable that Askin, Askins, and Haskins are thus derived; v. Askin.

headwords.meaning: the son of Anastasia, from the nick. Anstie (v. Anstee), abbreviated to Astie
headwords.author_comment: There can be little doubt that this is the true solution. It has never been a common surname, and at present I can find representatives only in the United States. But this is not a rare occurrence.

headwords.meaning: the son of Austin, an early variant
headwords.author_comment: Of course the majority of the representatives of these variants of Austin are now lost in the local surname Aston, q.v. This was inevitable, hence the scarcity of modern instances. That Astin is a variant of Austin is settled by two entries concerning the same individual; v. Aust. The dim. Austiline is also found.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 1, 0, 0; London, 0, 1, 1; Boston (U.S.), 0, 1, 0; New York, 1, 11, 0

headwords.meaning: of Asthill
headwords.author_comment: The suffix is commonly turned into 'le' or 'ell'; cf. Tickle for Tickhill, Buckell for Buckhill. For another origin v. Astell.

headwords.meaning: of Astley: (1) a chapelry in the parish of Leigh, co. Lanc.; (2) a chapelry in the county of Salop, five miles from Shrewsbury; (3) a parish in co. Warwick, near Nuneaton; (4) a parish in co. Worcester, near Stourport
headwords.author_comment: The Lancashire Astleys are all from the chapelry near Leigh in that county.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Aston or Ashton (v. Ashton); (2) the son of Astin (v. Astin)
headwords.author_comment: That Astin became Aston is clear from three entries in the same village.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Adam; (2) the son of Archibald; v. Aitcheson and Adkin
at the fen
headwords.author_comment: The final d in Atfend is excrescent; cf. gownd for gown, or Simmonds for Simmons, or Hamond for Hamon.

headwords.meaning: at the ford, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Attwood, Attwell, &c. I cannot find any modern representatives, but doubtless some exist.

headwords.meaning: 'atte-haws', from residence beside the haws
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Attwood, Attwell, Athow, &c., and v. Hawe.

headwords.meaning: see Adderley
of Atherton, a chapelry in the parish of Leigh, co. Lanc.
headwords.author_comment: The Boston Directory shows that the name crossed the Atlantic some generations ago.

headwords.meaning: at the how; v. How
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Attwell, Attwood, &c., for 'at the well,' 'at the wood,' &c. With the variant Attoe, cf. Hoo and Hoe, q.v. The Lincolnshire variant Ato, although curious to look at, is perfectly plain as regards its parentage.

headwords.meaning: see Adkin
'at the kirk' or 'church', from residence thereby; v. Kirk and Church
headwords.author_comment: Atkirk, unlike Attwood or Attwell, seems to have become extinct; but Achurch, abbreviated from Atte-Church, still exists. This, however, may represent Achurch, a township in co. Northampton.

headwords.meaning: at the oak; A.S. ác
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Acton, Ackworth, Ackroyd, acorn, &c., and v. Attwood, Attwell, &c.
headwords.modern_distribution: MDB. (Cambridge), 0, 1, 0, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 1, 0, 0, 0; Philadelphia, 0, 0, 2, 2

headwords.meaning: (1) of Attenborough, a parish in co. Notts; (2) of Attleburgh, a town in co. Norf.; (3) 'at the borough' or 'bury' (v. Bury)
headwords.author_comment: I have placed Attenborough and Atterbury together, as they have probably become confused in the course of centuries. In any case Atterbury represents the older Attleburgh. v. Bury.

headwords.meaning: at the slough, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: v. Slough, where manifest proof is given; cf. Attwood, Attwell, &c.

headwords.meaning: at the field, from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: cf. Attwood, Attwell, &c.; v. Field.

headwords.meaning: at the hill, from residence thereon
headwords.author_comment: v. Hill; cf. Attwell, Attwood, &c. This surname has existed in co. Norfolk for at least five centuries.
